question.problem:
According to the Chinese remainder theorem, which of the following systems of congruences has a unique solution modulo $60?$ 

$$
\text{I.}\,\{\begin{aligned}x≡1 & (\text{mod}\,3) \\ x≡2 & (\text{mod}\,4) \\ x≡3 & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}\,\text{II.}\,\{\begin{aligned}x≡3 & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ x≡2 & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}\,\text{III.}\,\{\begin{aligned}x≡2 & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x≡3 & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}\,
$$
question.worked_solution:
The Chinese remainder theorem states that if the natural numbers ${n}_{1},{n}_{2},…,{n}_{k}$ are pairwise coprime, meaning that $\text{gcd}({n}_{i},{n}_{j})=1$ whenever $i\ne j,$ then for any integers ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},…,{a}_{k}$ the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x≡{a}_{1} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{1}) \\ x≡{a}_{2} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{2}) \\ \,⋮ \\ x≡{a}_{k} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{k})\end{aligned}
$$

has a unique solution modulo ${n}_{1}{n}_{2}⋯{n}_{k}.$

Let's now inspect each of the given systems in turn.

- The theorem applies to system I. The numbers $3,$ $4,$ and $5$ are pairwise coprime natural numbers. Therefore, according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $3\cdot 4\cdot 5=60.$

- The theorem does *not* apply to system II since $6$ and $10$ are not coprime: 

$$
\text{gcd}(6,10)=2>1
$$

- The theorem applies to system III. The numbers $5$ and $12$ are pairwise coprime natural numbers. Therefore, according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $5\cdot 12=60.$

So, the correct answer is "I and III only."
